title: Anthony Fauci and public health
text:
It is difficult for me to watch and follow the travails that Dr Fauci is being put through. Fauci is a public health researcher at the NIH who came to fame during the AIDS epidemic of the 1980s and happened to be the administrator in charge of the NIH during the Covid-19 pandemic.  The legal jeopardy that he is facing (and the limits of a pardon and invoking the 5th amendment), in my view, is unwarranted and represents vindictiveness of the political right. However, there are legitimate scientific and research issues that are worthy of honest discussion and debate.

What is central is the concept of "gain-of-function" research on viruses. Gain-of-function (GOF) research is laboratory research in which scientists deliberately alter an organism—most commonly a virus—to give it new or enhanced biological properties. Those properties might include:

Greater ability to infect cells or animals
Increased transmissibility
Ability to evade immunity
Resistance to antiviral drugs
Changes in the range of species it can infect (host range)
Occasionally, increased virulence (ability to cause disease)

The term sounds alarming, but in biology it is actually quite broad. Scientists have performed gain-of-function experiments for decades in bacteria, yeast, plants, mice, and viruses. The controversy centers on a small subset involving pathogens that could pose a pandemic risk.

Today, much U.S. oversight focuses on a narrower category than gain-of-function research in general.

Research receives heightened scrutiny if it is reasonably anticipated to create or enhance a pathogen that is both:

Highly transmissible or likely to spread widely, and
Likely to cause severe disease in humans.

Not all gain-of-function research falls into this category.

Scientifically:

Many virologists dislike the term "gain-of-function" because it encompasses an enormous range of routine molecular biology experiments.
Biosafety experts instead focus on whether an experiment is reasonably expected to create an enhanced potential pandemic pathogen, since that more directly captures the level of concern.

The central policy question is not whether scientists should ever modify viruses—they do so routinely in legitimate research—but where society should draw the line between the potential public-health benefits and the small but potentially catastrophic risks of creating more dangerous pathogens. That balance, rather than the phrase "gain of function" itself, remains the heart of the debate.

The whole Covid-19 episode and subsequent politics have undermined research and expertise in the setting of limited data and an evolving knowledgebase.  By definition, scientific method evolves its assumptions based on new data. Criminalizing public health decisions sends a chilling message. IMHO.
